newsitem.title: BOSNIA: US says Serbs to sack war crimes suspects from police.
newsitem.headline: US says Serbs to sack war crimes suspects from police.

text.p: Bosnian Serb leader Biljana Plavsic has promised to sack four policemen indicted by the international war crimes tribunal on former Yugoslavia, a senior U.S. official said on Monday.

But John Shattuck, U.S. assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, said Plavsic baulked at handing over the four and other Serb indictees to the tribunal in The Hague for trial.
Shattuck was briefing reporters midway through four days of talks with Serb, Moslem and Croat leaders on unfulfilled human rights provisions of the 1995 Dayton peace treaty on Bosnia.

He said he warned Serb and Croat officials in particular that continuing to flout obligations to relinquish war-crimes indictees would cost them vital reconstruction aid from the West, aside from hindering ethnic reconciliation.

"I received a commitment from (Plavsic) that the four individuals now serving in the police department in Prijedor will be fired," Shattuck said when asked what his meeting with the nationalist Bosnian Serb president on Sunday produced.
"I indicated to her that this was not sufficient, that they and other indicted war criminals must be brought to justice in The Hague ... (But Plavsic made) very insufficient guarantees.
"I made clear to her that if there were not better guarantees there would be negative political and economic consequences," the U.S. human rights supremo said.
Plavsic had argued that the Serb republic's constitution ruled out extradition of its citizens abroad but Shattuck said this was no excuse for ignoring international law.

He said he drove similar points home in talks with Bosnian Croat leader Kresimir Zubak. Croats control part of a shaky Federation with Moslems that covers half of Bosnia. The other half is a Bosnian Serb Republic.

Over two thirds of 75 tribunal indictees are Serbs, including wartime political leader Radovan Karadzic and army chief General Ratko Mladic, while 18 are Croats. Less than 10 are in custody, most of them apprehended in Western Europe.
The Prijedor policemen were indicted for atrocities against Moslem prisoners in several notorious detention camps run in the Serb-held north at the start of the war in 1992.

Croatia armed Bosnian Croats in their 1993-94 separatist war and is held responsible by the West for Croat defiance of the tribunal. Shattuck said he would meet Croatian President Franjo Tudjman about the problem on Tuesday.

Shattuck will go to Belgrade on Wednesday to lean on President Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia for action as well. He has disregarded repeated appeals to surrender three ex-Yugoslav army officers indicted for massacres of Croats in Croatia's 1991 war for independence from federal Yugoslavia.
Shattuck has made several previous trips to the region to push for compliance with the tribunal, to no avail.

Asked how he could expect the parties to be more responsive this time unless the NATO peace force in Bosnia, whose mandate is now being re-defined by alliance planners, were empowered to hunt down indictees, he said:

"You are well aware there are discussions under way on that subject (new mandate) now. ... We are entering a new phase in the implementation of the peace process, so for that reason the urgency of compliance is being underscored more than ever."

Carl Bildt, international peace coordinator in Bosnia, has suggested the world stop relying entirely on ex-war factions to uphold the tribunal's mission, perpetuating "a mismatch between rhetoric and realities on the ground".
"We must look at ways of creating (enforcement) instruments ... to ensure that one faction or another simply does not make a complete mockery of the international community," he said.
